1.title: A Second Prophet
1.context: The eighth month of Darius's second year is late 520 BC. Zechariah worked alongside Haggai, and Ezra 5:1 names the two together as the prophets who stirred the rebuilding of the temple. Iddo appears among the priestly families who returned from Babylon, so Zechariah was probably a priest as well as a prophet.
1.question: Haggai spoke to the builders' hands and Zechariah to their hearts. Which of the two needs the word in you today?

1.title: Return to Me
1.context: The title the LORD of Hosts is used more than fifty times in this short book. The offer to return echoes the covenant language of Deuteronomy and the earlier prophets; Malachi 3:7 repeats it almost word for word a generation later.
1.question: What would returning look like for you this week, in one concrete step rather than a feeling?

1.title: Where Are Your Fathers Now?
1.context: The former prophets are the preachers before the exile, such as Isaiah, Jeremiah and Hosea, who called Judah to turn from its evil ways. The rhetorical questions point out that both the hearers and the preachers of that age are now dead, while their message has proved true.
1.question: Whose warnings in your own family story do you now see were right?

1.title: The Word That Overtook Them
1.context: The verb overtake pictures God's words as a pursuer catching up with those who ran from them. The confession at the end of the verse is the kind of admission found in Lamentations and in the prayers of Daniel 9 and Nehemiah 9.
1.question: Where has a word you resisted caught up with you, and what did it teach you?

1.title: Memory Before Mystery
1.context: This short sermon introduces the whole book: the visions of 1:7–6:15, the question about fasting in chapters 7–8, and the two burdens of chapters 9–14 all assume a people who have heard the call to return.
1.question: Before you ask God to show you something new, what has He already said that you have not yet answered?

2.title: A Rider Among the Myrtles
2.context: The date is February of 519 BC, and the eight night visions that follow all seem to come in this one night. Myrtles were low evergreen shrubs that grew in valleys. The interpreting angel who explains each vision to Zechariah is a feature of this book and of Daniel.
2.question: Zechariah asks God what he is seeing. What would you ask if you could ask one question about your situation?

2.title: All the Earth Is at Rest
2.context: By 519 BC Darius had put down the revolts that followed his accession, and the Persian Empire was settled again. The riders' report of a quiet earth describes that peace, which left Judah small and its temple unfinished.
2.question: When everything around you is calm but something you care about is still broken, how do you pray?

2.title: How Long, O LORD?
2.context: How long is the lament of the Psalms (Psalm 13; 74; 79). The seventy years recall Jeremiah 25:11–12 and 29:10, the period Daniel 9:2 reflects on. Counting from the temple's destruction in 586 BC, about seventy years had passed by 519 BC.
2.question: What have you been asking God how long about? Can you say it to Him plainly, as the angel does?

2.title: Kind and Comforting Words
2.context: Jealous here is covenant language: the passion of God for His own people, not envy. The nations at ease had been instruments of judgment, as Isaiah 10 and 47 also describe, but went beyond what God intended and added to the calamity.
2.question: Does it comfort you or unsettle you that God speaks of being jealous for His people?

2.title: My House Will Be Rebuilt
2.context: A measuring line stretched out is a builder's preparation, the opposite of the line of destruction in 2 Kings 21:13 and Lamentations 2:8. The temple was finished in 516 BC, about three years after this vision, as Ezra 6:15 records.
2.question: What in your life does God seem to be measuring out to rebuild rather than to judge?

3.title: Four Horns
3.context: In Hebrew Bibles these verses begin chapter 2, so references can differ between translations; the BSB follows the English numbering. Horns stand for military strength, as in Psalm 75 and Daniel 7–8. The number four suggests completeness, the scattering powers of every direction.
3.question: What powers have scattered you or the people you love?

3.title: Four Craftsmen
3.context: The Hebrew word for craftsmen covers workers in wood, stone and metal. The vision does not say who they are; the point is that for every power raised against God's people He has a worker ready to bring it down.
3.question: Where might God answer a hard power in your life with patient workmanship instead of force?

3.title: A City Without Walls
3.context: Walled cities were the norm in the ancient world, and Nehemiah would rebuild Jerusalem's walls about seventy years later. The promise of a wall of fire recalls the pillar of fire in the exodus, and the glory within looks back to the glory that filled the tabernacle and temple.
3.question: What walls are you trying to build for yourself that God offers to be instead?

3.title: Flee from the Land of the North
3.context: Babylon lay to the east, but armies and travelers reached Judah from the north along the Fertile Crescent, so the north stands for Babylon here. Many Judeans stayed in Babylon after Cyrus allowed the return. The apple of His eye is the pupil, the most protected part of the eye, as in Deuteronomy 32:10.
3.question: Who in your life needs to hear that touching them touches the apple of God's eye?

3.title: I Am Coming to Dwell Among You
3.context: The phrase Holy Land appears only here in the Old Testament (2:12). The promise that many nations will join the LORD looks ahead to chapter 8 and echoes Isaiah 2 and 56. The call to silence echoes Habakkuk 2:20 and Zephaniah 1:7.
3.question: What would it take for you to be silent before the LORD today, even for a few minutes?

4.title: The Accuser at His Right Hand
4.context: Satan here means the accuser and has the definite article, as in Job 1–2: a title describing his role in the heavenly court. Joshua son of Jehozadak was high priest at the return (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1); his father had been carried into exile (1 Chronicles 6:15).
4.question: What accusations do you hear most often against yourself?

4.title: A Firebrand Snatched from the Fire
4.context: Amos 4:11 uses the same picture of a burning stick pulled from the fire. Filthy garments would disqualify a priest from service, since the priestly clothing of Exodus 28 was for glory and beauty. Joshua stands for a priesthood and people stained by exile and sin.
4.question: What does it mean to you that God's answer to the accuser begins with His choice, not your record?

4.title: Splendid Robes and a Clean Turban
4.context: The high priest's turban carried a gold plate inscribed HOLY TO THE LORD (Exodus 28:36–38), a phrase that returns in Zechariah 14:20. Isaiah 61:10 uses similar language of God clothing His people with garments of salvation.
4.question: What would you need God to take off you, and what would you ask Him to put on?

4.title: If You Walk in My Ways
4.context: Access among these who are standing here means a place in the heavenly council among the angels attending God. The companions seated before Joshua are probably his fellow priests.
4.question: Which responsibility God has given you calls for daily faithfulness rather than one decision?

4.title: My Servant, the Branch
4.context: The Branch is a royal title from Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 for a coming righteous king of David's line; Isaiah 11:1 uses a related image. Interpreters differ over the stone with seven eyes, whether it is a foundation stone, a gem or a symbol of God's watchfulness (compare 4:10). Sitting under one's own vine and fig tree is an image of peace from 1 Kings 4:25 and Micah 4:4.
4.question: Who could you invite to sit with you this week in a place of peace?

5.title: A Lampstand and Two Olive Trees
5.context: The lampstand recalls the golden lampstand of the tabernacle (Exodus 25:31–40), but this one has a bowl as a reservoir and is supplied directly by two olive trees. The repeated question and answer is part of the vision's teaching method.
5.question: What would you need to admit you do not know before God can show you something?

5.title: Not by Might nor by Power
5.context: Zerubbabel, a grandson of King Jehoiachin, was the Persian-appointed governor of Judah (Haggai 1:1). The great mountain probably stands for the obstacles to finishing the temple, including the local opposition recorded in Ezra 4–5. The capstone is the final stone set in place.
5.question: What mountain in front of you are you trying to move by might or power?

5.title: His Hands Will Complete It
5.context: Ezra 3:8–11 records the laying of the foundation in the second year after the return, around 536 BC. The work then stopped until 520 BC. Ezra 6:14–15 records the completion in 516 BC, the sixth year of Darius.
5.question: What did you begin for God that stalled, and what would finishing it require?

5.title: The Day of Small Things
5.context: The plumb line was a builder's weight on a cord for checking that walls were straight. Ezra 3:12 tells of older people weeping when they saw the new foundation and remembered Solomon's temple; Haggai 2:3 addresses the same disappointment.
5.question: What small beginning in your life have you been tempted to despise?

5.title: The Two Anointed Ones
5.context: The Hebrew calls them sons of oil. Most interpreters identify them with Zerubbabel the governor and Joshua the high priest, the royal and priestly leaders of the community; Revelation 11:4 takes up the image of two olive trees and two lampstands.
5.question: Who are the people God has set beside you to keep your lamp supplied?

6.title: A Flying Scroll
6.context: Twenty by ten cubits is about thirty by fifteen feet, the size of Solomon's temple porch (1 Kings 6:3) and of the holy place in the tabernacle. Theft and false swearing stand for the two parts of the law, duties toward neighbor and toward God.
6.question: Which side of the scroll, honesty with people or honesty before God, searches you more?

6.title: It Will Enter the House
6.context: The curse is the covenant sanction of Deuteronomy 28 and Leviticus 26 for breaking the law. Destroying a house down to its timbers and stones recalls the treatment of a house with mildew in Leviticus 14:45.
6.question: What would you not want a scroll like this to find in your house?

6.title: Wickedness in a Basket
6.context: The measuring basket is an ephah, a dry measure of roughly twenty liters. A lead cover, a heavy talent of lead, seals it shut. Personifying wickedness as a woman is a symbolic device in the vision, not a statement about women.
6.question: What wrong do you need God to seal up and carry away rather than just restrain?

6.title: A House in Shinar
6.context: Shinar is the old name for the plain of Babylon, where the tower of Babel was built (Genesis 11:2). The stork was an unclean bird under the law (Leviticus 11:19), fitting carriers for this cargo. The pedestal suggests an idol set up in a temple.
6.question: What has God already carried away from your life that you are grateful never to have back?

6.title: Two Households
6.context: Chapters 5 and 6 together describe the purifying of the restored community. Cleansing the land of sin before God's presence returns follows the pattern of the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 16, where the scapegoat carries the people's sins away.
6.question: Which house is growing in you right now, God's house or the one being built for something else?

7.title: Chariots Between Bronze Mountains
7.context: The two mountains of bronze may picture the gateway of God's dwelling. The horse colors echo the first vision (1:8) and the riders of Revelation 6. This eighth vision forms a frame with the first.
7.question: Where do you need reminding that God's purposes are moving even when you cannot see them?

7.title: Rest for My Spirit in the North
7.context: The Hebrew word for spirits can also mean winds, as in 2:6. The north again stands for Babylon. Giving rest to God's Spirit there probably means His anger toward Babylon is satisfied, or that He has moved the exiles there to return.
7.question: Where are you waiting for God's Spirit to settle something that troubles you?

7.title: A Crown from the Exiles
7.context: Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah are otherwise unknown returnees who had brought gifts from Babylon. Crowning a priest was unusual, since crowns belonged to kings; setting the crown on Joshua rather than Zerubbabel the governor may have avoided the appearance of rebellion against Persia, and it made the act a sign.
7.question: What have you been given that God might want turned into a sign of His promises?

7.title: A Priest on His Throne
7.context: The Branch is the royal title from 3:8 and Jeremiah 23:5. In Israel kingship and priesthood were kept separate (2 Chronicles 26:16–21). Psalm 110:4 speaks of a king who is a priest forever, and the New Testament letter to the Hebrews develops this theme.
7.question: What does it mean to you that the promised ruler is also a priest?

7.title: A Memorial in the Temple
7.context: Helem is probably another name for Heldai, and the gracious son of Zephaniah is Josiah of verse 10. The crown was kept as a memorial, and the closing condition repeats Deuteronomy 28:1.
7.question: What memorial of God's promise could you keep where you would see it often?

8.title: A Delegation from Bethel
8.context: The date is December of 518 BC. Bethel lay about twelve miles north of Jerusalem. The fast in the fifth month remembered the burning of the temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8–9).
8.question: What habit of mourning or discipline have you kept long after asking why you keep it?

8.title: Was It Really for Me?
8.context: The fast of the seventh month remembered the murder of Gedaliah, the governor appointed after Jerusalem fell (2 Kings 25:25; Jeremiah 41). Isaiah 58 asks the same question about fasting that changes nothing.
8.question: If God asked whether your religious practices were really for Him, how would you answer?

8.title: What the Earlier Prophets Said
8.context: The Negev is the dry southern region of Judah, and the foothills, the Shephelah, lay to the west. The call to true justice and loving devotion repeats Micah 6:8 and Hosea 6:6. Loving devotion translates hesed, God's covenant love.
8.question: Where could you show loving devotion and compassion to someone this week?

8.title: Hearts Like Flint
8.context: Widows, orphans, foreigners and the poor are the vulnerable people the law protects again and again (Exodus 22:21–24; Deuteronomy 24:17). Turning a stubborn shoulder pictures an ox refusing the yoke. Flint was the hardest stone known.
8.question: Which of these four groups is closest to you right now, and what do they need?

8.title: Scattered with a Whirlwind
8.context: The measure-for-measure pattern echoes Proverbs 1:24–28 and Jeremiah 11:11. The whirlwind pictures the sudden scattering of the exile. The pleasant land is a name for Canaan found in Jeremiah 3:19 and Psalm 106:24.
8.question: Is there a call from God you have been not listening to?

9.title: Jealous for Zion
9.context: Chapter 8 collects ten short oracles, each beginning with a form of thus says the LORD of Hosts. City of Truth can also be translated the faithful city, recalling Isaiah 1:21 and 26.
9.question: What would it mean for God to give your city, or your home, the name Truth?

9.title: Boys and Girls Playing
9.context: Sieges and deportations fell hardest on the old and the young (Lamentations 2:11, 21). Long life and children in the streets were signs of covenant blessing. The rhetorical question echoes Genesis 18:14, is anything too hard for the LORD?
9.question: What promise of God feels too large for your present circumstances?

9.title: Let Your Hands Be Strong
9.context: Before those days refers to the years before the work resumed in 520 BC, the hardship Haggai 1:6–11 describes. A curse among the nations is a byword for disaster (Jeremiah 24:9); being a blessing recalls the promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:2.
9.question: Where do you need to hear do not be afraid, let your hands be strong?

9.title: Fasts Become Feasts
9.context: The four fasts marked stages of Jerusalem's fall: the breach of the walls in the fourth month, the temple's burning in the fifth, Gedaliah's murder in the seventh, and the start of the siege in the tenth (2 Kings 25; Jeremiah 39–41). This answers the Bethel delegation's question of 7:3.
9.question: What sorrow of yours do you most long to see turned into a feast?

9.title: Let Us Go with You
9.context: Ten men from every language is a way of saying a great many, from every nation. Grasping the corner of a robe was a gesture of earnest appeal. The picture echoes Isaiah 2:2–3 and Micah 4:1–2, the nations streaming to Jerusalem to learn God's ways.
9.question: Who around you might say they have heard that God is with you?

10.title: The Burden Against Damascus
10.context: A burden is a heavy prophetic message, often of judgment, a heading also used in Nahum, Habakkuk and Malachi. Chapters 9–14 carry no dates, and scholars debate when they were written. Tyre's island fortress withstood a thirteen-year siege by Nebuchadnezzar and fell to Alexander the Great in 332 BC.
10.question: What security are you tempted to heap up for yourself like Tyre's silver?

10.title: A Remnant for Our God
10.context: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron and Ashdod were cities of the Philistines, Israel's longtime enemies. Blood and abominations in their mouths refers to eating sacrificial meat with the blood, forbidden by the law. The Jebusites held Jerusalem before David and were absorbed into Israel (2 Samuel 5:6–9; 24:18–24).
10.question: Who do you find it hardest to imagine God welcoming into His people?

10.title: Your King Comes to You
10.context: Rulers rode donkeys and mules in times of peace (Judges 10:4; 1 Kings 1:33), while horses meant war. All four Gospels connect this verse with Jesus' entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:5; John 12:15). The dominion from sea to sea echoes Psalm 72:8.
10.question: What does it mean to you that the King comes humble, and how does that change how you welcome Him?

10.title: Prisoners of Hope
10.context: The blood of My covenant recalls the covenant ceremony at Sinai (Exodus 24:8). Dry cisterns were used as prisons; Joseph (Genesis 37:24) and Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:6) were both thrown into one. Double was the restoration promised in Isaiah 61:7.
10.question: In what situation are you being asked to be a prisoner of hope?

10.title: Like Jewels in a Crown
10.context: Greece here is Javan, the Hebrew name for the Greek peoples of the Aegean and western Asia Minor. Some interpreters connect the verse with the later Greek empires; others read it more broadly of distant nations. The ram's horn, the shofar, was blown in battle and worship.
10.question: What would it look like for God to treat you as one of the jewels in His crown?

11.title: Ask the LORD for Rain
11.context: Judah depended on the autumn and spring rains. Household idols, teraphim, were consulted for guidance (compare Ezekiel 21:21), a practice the law forbade. Sheep without a shepherd is an old picture of leaderless people (Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17).
11.question: Where do you go first for help when you are anxious, and what does that show you?

11.title: Shepherds Judged, a Flock Raised Up
11.context: Shepherds is a common term for kings and leaders in the ancient world and in Ezekiel 34. Cornerstone, tent peg and battle bow are images of stable, reliable leadership coming from Judah itself; the New Testament also calls the Messiah the cornerstone, drawing on Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 28:16.
11.question: Who in your life is a cornerstone or a tent peg, someone others can lean on?

11.title: As Though I Had Not Rejected Them
11.context: The house of Joseph means the northern tribes, also called Ephraim, scattered by Assyria in 722 BC. Their return alongside Judah echoes Ezekiel 37:15–28, where two sticks become one.
11.question: What would it mean to you to live as though God had not rejected you, because He has not?

11.title: I Will Whistle for Them
11.context: The whistle is a shepherd's or beekeeper's signal (Isaiah 5:26; 7:18). Gilead lay east of the Jordan and Lebanon to the north, the edges of the old promised land. Passing through the sea of distress recalls the crossing of the Red Sea at the exodus.
11.question: Where have you seen God gather back what had been scattered?

11.title: In His Name They Will Walk
11.context: To walk in God's name means to live by His character and under His authority, as in Micah 4:5. The verse sums up the chapter's contrast between those who trust idols and diviners and those strengthened by the LORD.
11.question: What would walking in His name change about how you go through tomorrow?

12.title: Lebanon's Cedars Burn
12.context: Cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan were the grandest trees the Israelites knew, and they often stand for proud rulers (Isaiah 2:13). The thickets of the Jordan were the dense jungle along the river where lions lived (Jeremiah 12:5).
12.question: What proud thing in your life might God need to bring down before He can shepherd you?

12.title: The Flock Marked for Slaughter
12.context: In this passage the prophet acts out a part, a sign act like those of Ezekiel 4–5 and Jeremiah 13. Interpreters differ on whether he describes real events in his own day or an enacted parable of Israel's history.
12.question: Where have you seen people treated as a commodity, and how did it make you feel?

12.title: Two Staffs, Favor and Union
12.context: Shepherds carried a rod and a staff (Psalm 23:4). The names Favor and Union describe God's grace toward the flock and the unity of the people. The identity of the three shepherds dismissed in one month is one of the most debated questions in the book.
12.question: Which do you need more today, God's favor or unity with others?

12.title: Thirty Pieces of Silver
12.context: Thirty shekels was the compensation set for a slave gored by an ox (Exodus 21:32). Throwing it to the potter may mean to the temple workshop, or it may be an idiom for contempt. Matthew 27:9–10 connects this passage with Judas's thirty pieces of silver.
12.question: What value have you placed on God's care for you, and what would honor it?

12.title: The Worthless Shepherd
12.context: The foolish shepherd is the opposite of the good shepherd of Ezekiel 34:16, who seeks the lost and binds up the injured. The arm stands for strength and the right eye for watchfulness, both of which the worthless shepherd loses.
12.question: Who depends on you to seek, heal or sustain them, and how are you caring for them?

13.title: A Cup of Drunkenness
13.context: The second burden covers chapters 12–14 and repeats the phrase on that day many times. The cup of staggering is an image of God's judgment on nations (Isaiah 51:17–23; Jeremiah 25:15–29).
13.question: What heavy stone in your life have you tried to lift that only God can carry?

13.title: The Tents of Judah First
13.context: Panic, madness and blindness echo the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:28, here turned against the attacking nations. A firepot carried coals for lighting fires. Saving Judah's countryside first keeps the royal city from boasting over the towns.
13.question: Where are you tempted to think your place matters more than someone else's?

13.title: The One They Have Pierced
13.context: The shift from Me to Him in the same verse has puzzled readers for centuries, and some ancient copies and translations smooth it out. John 19:37 applies the verse to the crucifixion of Jesus, and Revelation 1:7 echoes it. Mourning for an only child was the deepest grief in Israel (Amos 8:10).
13.question: What does it mean to you that grace leads to grief here, and grief to cleansing?

13.title: Each Clan on Its Own
13.context: Hadad-rimmon is probably a place near Megiddo where King Josiah was killed in 609 BC and mourned by all Judah (2 Chronicles 35:22–25). Nathan was a son of David and Shimei a grandson of Levi (Numbers 3:17–18), so the list pairs royal and priestly families.
13.question: What grief do you carry that you need to bring to God in private?

13.title: The Seam Left Open
13.context: Zechariah 12–14 is among the Old Testament passages the New Testament quotes most often in telling the story of Jesus' death. The prophet himself does not explain the piercing.
13.question: What question about God are you willing to leave open while still trusting Him?

14.title: A Fountain Opened
14.context: Impurity here translates a word used for ritual uncleanness in the law (Numbers 19). Ezekiel 36:25 and 47:1–12 also picture cleansing water flowing from God, and the theme returns in Zechariah 14:8.
14.question: What do you need cleansed that you cannot wash away yourself?

14.title: The Names of the Idols Erased
14.context: Deuteronomy 13:1–11 and 18:20 command the death of a prophet who leads people astray, even by family members. The hairy cloak was the mark of a prophet, worn by Elijah (2 Kings 1:8) and later by John the Baptist.
14.question: What false voice in your life would you like God to silence?

14.title: Wounds in the House of My Friends
14.context: Ecstatic prophets sometimes cut themselves, as the prophets of Baal did on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:28). The man's denial echoes Amos 7:14, where Amos says he was no prophet but a herdsman. Interpreters debate whether the wounds are self-inflicted or received elsewhere.
14.question: When have you been tempted to hide what you really are or have done?

14.title: Strike the Shepherd
14.context: Companion translates a rare word for a close associate or equal. Jesus quotes this verse on the night of His arrest, applying it to Himself and His disciples (Matthew 26:31; Mark 14:27).
14.question: What does it mean to you that this Shepherd is struck by God's own command?

14.title: Refined Like Silver
14.context: Refining silver and testing gold by fire is an image of purifying suffering in Isaiah 48:10 and Malachi 3:2–3. They are My people and the LORD is our God is the covenant formula of Hosea 2:23 and Jeremiah 31:33.
14.question: What fire in your life might God be using to refine rather than to destroy?

15.title: A Day of the LORD Is Coming
15.context: The day of the LORD is a prophetic term for a decisive time of judgment and rescue (Amos 5:18; Joel 2; Zephaniah 1). Interpreters differ on whether this chapter describes particular historical events, the end of history, or both.
15.question: What helps you trust God when the worst actually happens?

15.title: His Feet on the Mount of Olives
15.context: The Mount of Olives rises east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley; Ezekiel 11:23 saw God's glory leave the city by way of it. The earthquake in Uzziah's day is the one dated in Amos 1:1. Light at evening breaks the usual order of day and night.
15.question: Where do you most need to believe that at evening there will be light?

15.title: Living Water and One King
15.context: The Eastern Sea is the Dead Sea and the Western Sea the Mediterranean. Living water means flowing water, as in Ezekiel 47:1–12. The LORD alone and His name alone echoes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4. Geba and Rimmon marked Judah's northern and southern limits.
15.question: What would it mean for the LORD alone to be King over your life?

15.title: Up Year After Year
15.context: The Feast of Tabernacles, or Booths, was the autumn harvest festival remembering Israel's wilderness journey (Leviticus 23:33–43). Rain was given in that season, which is why its withholding is the penalty. Egypt, watered by the Nile rather than rain, is named separately.
15.question: What harvest of God's goodness could you celebrate this year?

15.title: Holy to the LORD
15.context: HOLY TO THE LORD was engraved on the high priest's turban plate (Exodus 28:36). Canaanite can also mean trader or merchant in Hebrew, so the last verse may mean no more traffickers in the temple; compare Jesus clearing the temple in John 2:16.
15.question: What ordinary thing in your life, like a cooking pot, could become holy to the LORD?
